claim: T-REX identified rhinovirus-specific CD4+ T cells based on phenotypically homogeneous cells expanding by ≥95% following infection.
source: T-REX identified rhinovirus-specific CD4+ T cells based on phenotypically homogeneous cells expanding by ≥95% following infection.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing T-REX identified cells with ≥95% expansion that were enriched for tetramer+ virus-specific cells in rhinovirus infection studies.

claim: T-REX successfully identified hotspots of virus-specific T cells by comparing infection (day 7) to either pre-infection (day 0) or post-infection (day 28) samples.
source: T-REX successfully identified hotspots of virus-specific T cells by comparing infection (day 7) to either pre-infection (day 0) or post-infection (day 28) samples.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from multiple timepoint comparisons showing T-REX identified tetramer+ hotspots in both day 0 vs day 7 and day 7 vs day 28 comparisons.

claim: The magnitude and direction of change in some COVID-19 patients was comparable to blast crisis acute myeloid leukemia patients undergoing a complete response to chemotherapy.
source: For example, the magnitude and direction of change in some COVID-19 patients was comparable to blast crisis acute myeloid leukemia patients undergoing a complete response to chemotherapy.
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis of degree and direction of change across disease types, showing some COVID-19 patients had similar patterns to AML responders.

claim: Other COVID-19 patients displayed an immune trajectory like that seen in rhinovirus infection or checkpoint inhibitor therapy for melanoma.
source: Other COVID-19 patients instead displayed an immune trajectory like that seen in rhinovirus infection or checkpoint inhibitor therapy for melanoma.
evidence: The manuscript presents comparative analysis showing some COVID-19 patients had low magnitude of change similar to rhinovirus or melanoma checkpoint inhibitor therapy patients.

claim: Single cell analysis tools can struggle to reveal rare cells that are under 0.1% of the population.
source: However, single cell analysis tools can struggle to reveal rare cells that are under 0.1% of the population.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of existing tools and is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Viral immune and cancer immunotherapy responses can include mechanistically important and extremely rare T cells that proliferate rapidly over the course of days but as an aggregate exist as <0.1% of blood CD3+ T cells at their peak.
source: Viral immune and cancer immunotherapy responses can include mechanistically important and extremely rare T cells that proliferate rapidly over the course of days but as an aggregate exist as <0.1% of blood CD3+ T cells at their peak.
evidence: This statement is supported by the rhinovirus data presented in the manuscript showing tetramer+ cells at very low frequencies.

claim: Cytometry tools like SPADE, FlowSOM, Phenograph, Citrus, and RAPID generally work best to characterize cell subsets representing >1% of the sample.
source: Cytometry tools like SPADE (Bendall et al., 2011; Qiu et al., 2011), FlowSOM (Van Gassen et al., 2015), Phenograph (Levine et al., 2015), Citrus (Bruggner et al., 2014), and RAPID (Leelatian et al., 2020) generally work best to characterize cell subsets representing >1% of the sample and are less capable of capturing extremely rare cells or subsets distinguished by only a fraction of measured features.
evidence: This is stated based on known characteristics of these algorithms and supported by citations.

claim: Adults tend to have a stable signature of blood cell abundances over weeks to months in the absence of a perturbation such as disease or infection.
source: This T-REX design is based on the observation that, in the absence of a perturbation such as disease or infection, adults tend to have a stable signature of blood cell abundances over weeks to months (Greenplate et al., 2019; Lakshmikanth et al., 2020; Mathew et al., 2020), and the hypothesis that short-term, dramatic changes in rare immune cell subsets will identify cells associated with exposure to an immunogenic agent, such as a virus.
evidence: This observation is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Spectral flow cytometry generates data that compares well to mass cytometry.
source: Spectral flow cytometry is gaining attention in human immune monitoring as it generates data that compares well to mass cytometry (Ferrer-Font et al., 2020; Mistry et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Spectral flow cytometers collect cells at around 10-fold the number of cells per second as mass cytometers.
source: Spectral flow cytometers collect cells at around 10-fold the number of cells per second as mass cytometers.
evidence: This is stated as a known technical characteristic of the instruments.

claim: Mass cytometry commercial reagents presently allow 44 antibodies to be measured simultaneously per cell.
source: Mass cytometry is an established technique for human immune monitoring where commercial reagents presently allow 44 antibodies to be measured simultaneously per cell (Greenplate et al., 2016a; Mistry et al., 2019; Spitzer and Nolan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a current technical capability and supported by citations.

claim: Established spectral flow cytometry panels measure ~30 features per cell with excellent resolution.
source: While the availability of spectrally distinct antibody-fluorochrome conjugates imposes some practical limits on spectral flow cytometry at present, established panels like the one in Dataset 1 measure ~30 features per cell with excellent resolution, and that capacity is expected to roughly double in the next few years as recent work has demonstrated 40 features (Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated based on the panel used in Dataset 1 and supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Severe COVID-19 has been linked to a pathogenic 'cytokine storm' in which cellular immune responses likely play a crucial role.
source: Severe COVID-19 has been linked to a pathogenic 'cytokine storm' in which cellular immune responses likely play a crucial role (Ragab et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work on COVID-19 pathogenesis.

claim: Host factors are a key determinant of the degree of the T cell response in both rhinovirus and COVID-19.
source: Nonetheless, in the case of both rhinovirus and COVID-19, it is clear that host factors are a key determinant of the degree of the T cell response (Mathew et al., 2020; Muehling et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on both viruses.

claim: Infection with rhinovirus is known to induce expansion of circulating virus-specific CD4+ T cells in the blood.
source: Infection with rhinovirus is known to induce expansion of circulating virus-specific CD4+ T cells in the blood, and a key feature of the new rhinovirus dataset here is that rare and mechanistically important virus-specific CD4+ T cells were marked with MHC II tetramers in the context of multiple other T cell markers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about rhinovirus infection.

claim: A k-value of 60 was chosen for KNN analysis in T-REX based on optimization studies.
source: The k-value for KNN was set to 60 as a starting point based on prior studies and later optimized.
evidence: The manuscript describes optimization of k-value and selection of 60 based on analysis of tetramer enrichment.

claim: T-REX identified cells in regions of ≥95% change that were enriched for virus-specific cells in nearly all rhinovirus-infected individuals (4/6 at 95% cutoff, 5/6 at 85% cutoff).
source: Cells in regions of significant expansion (≥95%) were also from regions that were enriched for virus-specific cells in nearly all rhinovirus-infected individuals (4/6 at 95% cutoff, 5/6 at 85% cutoff) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The phenotype of rhinovirus-specific T cell regions identified by T-REX included activated memory cells (CD45RO+ CD38+) with early memory/stem-like T cell signature (TCF1+ CD27+) and expression of CCR5 and CXCR3.
source: The change hotspots thus contained activated memory cells (CD45RO + CD38+) that were notable for their early memory/stem-like T cell signature (TCF1+ CD27+), as well as their expression of CCR5 and CXCR3, both of which are chemokine receptors found on rhinovirus-specific CD4+ T cells that respond during infection (Muehling et al., 2020; Muehling et al., 2018).
evidence: This phenotype is derived from MEM analysis of T-REX identified cells and is consistent with prior studies cited.

claim: In analysis of RV001, T-REX captured 66.6% (2/3) of tetramer+ regions using a ≥95% change cutoff.
source: In analysis of RV001, 66.6% (2/3) of tetramer+ regions were captured, meaning there was one region with lower change that contained tetramer+ cells.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: T-REX captured the majority of virus-specific cells in the RV001 dataset, with 1722 cells in regions with ≥95% expansion compared to 87 cells in missed regions.
source: However, there were only 87 cells in these missed regions compared to 896 cells and 826 cells in the regions with ≥95% expansion, confirming that T-REX captured the majority of virus-specific cells in the dataset.
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of the analysis.

claim: A virtual FACS sorting strategy based on T-REX and MEM results successfully enriched for rhinovirus tetramer+ cells in all infected subjects (0.89‒9.25% of CD4+ T cells).
source: The 'virtual sort' successfully enriched for rhinovirus tetramer+ cells in all infected subjects (0.89‒9.25% of CD4+ T cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: Precursor frequencies of rhinovirus-specific CD4+ T cells are very low, even during active infection (0.0004‒0.04% of CD4+ T cells).
source: It is known that precursor frequencies of rhinovirus-specific CD4+ T cells are very low, even during active infection (0.0004‒0.04% of CD4+ T cells, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated as known information and supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: A minimal panel of 10 markers (Live, Dump–, CD3+, CD4+, CD45R0+, CD38+, ICOS+, CCR5+, PD-1+, CD95+) was sufficient to achieve maximal tetramer enrichment in the virtual sort.
source: A minimal panel of 10 markers (Live, Dump–, CD3+, CD4+, CD45R0+, CD38+, ICOS+, CCR5+, PD-1+, CD95+) was sufficient to achieve maximal tetramer enrichment.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the virtual sorting analysis.

claim: The T-REX-derived sorting strategy failed to enrich for rhinovirus-specific T cells in uninfected subjects and did not enrich for CD4+ T cells stained with a control influenza tetramer.
source: Furthermore, the T-REX-derived sorting strategy failed to enrich for rhinovirus-specific T cells in uninfected subject, nor did it enrich for CD4+ T cells stained with a control influenza tetramer, confirming the specificity of this method (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by control data in the referenced figure.

claim: Rhinovirus subjects had small changes in samples over time with a median degree of change of 0.019% and an interquartile range of 0.0006%.
source: Rhinovirus subjects had small changes in samples over time with a median of 0.019% and an interquartile range (IQR) of 0.0006%.
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of T-REX analysis.

claim: Rhinovirus subjects had large directionality across all subjects with a median of 0.029 and an IQR of 2.00.
source: Rhinovirus also had large directionality across all subjects either up or down, with a median of 0.029 and an IQR of 2.00.
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of T-REX analysis.

claim: COVID-19 samples varied from <1% to 68% in terms of degree of change, with a median of 6.86% and an IQR of 30.4%.
source: The COVID-19 samples varied from <1% to 68% in terms of degree of change, with a median of 6.86% and an IQR of 30.4%.
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of T-REX analysis of Dataset 2.

claim: The directionality of change in COVID-19 samples was near zero, with a median of –0.00880 and IQR of 0.773.
source: The directionality of change was near zero, with a median of –0.00880 and IQR of 0.773.
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of T-REX analysis of Dataset 2.

claim: COVID-19 patients with changes <5% generally had positive directionality (median of 0.55), whereas those with change >5% typically had negative directionality (median of –0.33).
source: Notably, the changes <5% were generally positive (median directionality of 0.55, N = 6), whereas the COVID-19 patient cell populations experiencing change >5% typically decreased between day 0 to day 7 (median directionality of –0.33, N = 6).
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of T-REX analysis of Dataset 2.

claim: In COVID-19 patient COV26, the largest population experiencing significant change had a phenotype indicating it was a CD14+ myeloid cell subset with high expression of CD147/Basigin.
source: For example, patient COV26 saw little change (magnitude of 2.02%) and this was almost entirely expansion (directionality of 0.99). The largest population experiencing significant change from COV26 decreased over time and had a MEM phenotype of CD147+10 CD99+8 CD29+6 CD38+4 CD55+3 CD14+2 CD39+2 CD64+1 CD56+1 CD8a+1, indicating that it was a CD14+ myeloid cell subset with high expression of CD147/Basigin.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of T-REX and MEM analysis of a specific patient.

claim: Of 10 COVID-19 patients analyzed for CD4+ T cells, 5 individuals had at least one hotspot of great change revealed by T-REX.
source: Of the 10 COVID-19 patients available for analysis, 5 individuals had at least one hotspot of great change, as revealed by T-REX, in CD4+ T cell-specific analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of T-REX analysis and supported by referenced figures.

claim: Four of five COVID-19 patients with CD4+ T cell hotspots had cells matching a consistent phenotype enriched for CD147, CD99, CD29, CD45, CD3, CD38, CD49d, CD52, CD27, CD28, and CD81.
source: Another phenotype of CD4+ T cells was consistently observed in those COVID-19 patients where T-REX revealed a hotspot. Of the five patients where T-REX identified a CD4+ T cell hotspot, four of the patients had a hotspot matching the aggregate phenotype (MEM label average and standard deviation: ▲CD147+9±0.8 CD99+9±1.3 CD29+8±1.3 CD45+4±2 CD3+4±0.7 CD38+4±1.8 CD49d+3±1.6 CD52+3±1 CD27+3±2.1 CD28+3±0.8 CD81+2±1.3 CD62L+2±1.2 CD56+2±0.7 CD5+2±0.6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of MEM analysis of T-REX identified cells across multiple patients.

claim: Manual biaxial gating using MEM-identified markers enriched CD4+ T cells from 5.5–14.0% to 49.6–83.3% of total cells in COVID-19 samples.
source: While CD4+ T cells only represented 5.5–14.0% of total cells, following MEM-based gating they were enriched to 49.6–83.3% of cells.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the virtual gating analysis.

claim: Melanoma samples in Dataset 3 for comparisons of day 21/35 vs. day 0 had a small degree of change (median of 0.58% and an IQR 2.34%) with varying directionality (median of –0.42 and an IQR of 1.46).
source: Overall, when analyzed by T-REX, the melanoma samples in Dataset 3 for comparisons of day 21/35 vs. day 0 had a small degree of change (median of 0.58% and an IQR 2.34%) with a varying directionality (median of –0.42 and an IQR of 1.46), confirming the subtle shifts in phenotypes as previously indicated.
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of T-REX analysis of Dataset 3.

claim: The majority of AML patients had a large degree of change in samples (median of 81.0% and an IQR of 75.2%) with little to no directionality (median of –0.00250 and an IQR of 0.0173).
source: As expected, the majority of AML patients had a large degree of change in samples (median of 81.0% and an IQR of 75.2%) with little to no directionality to the change (median of –0.00250 and an IQR of 0.0173), meaning that there were massive changes in terms of both expansion and contraction over the course of treatment.
evidence: This is directly stated as a quantitative result of T-REX analysis of Dataset 4.

claim: AML samples with a degree of change >80% came from patients with high blast count in the blood and complete response to treatment.
source: AML samples with a degree of change >80% (AML001, AML002, AML004) came from patients with high blast count in the blood and complete response to treatment, indicating the complete transformation of the immune environment after treatment.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result correlating T-REX metrics with clinical outcomes.

claim: T-REX using UMAP ran in 0.35 hr on the 1.3 million cell dataset from RV001 and identified a cluster that was 22% tetramer+.
source: This standard version of T-REX ran in 0.35 hr on the 1.3 million cell dataset from RV001 (Figure 7, left column) and identified a cluster that was 22% tetramer+.
evidence: This is directly stated as a performance benchmark and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: T-REX with t-SNE instead of UMAP resulted in a much longer runtime of 23 hr and comparable capture of areas of change, containing 22% tetramer+ cells.
source: An altered version of T-REX, in which t-SNE replaced UMAP as the method of dimensionality reduction, resulted in a much longer runtime of 23 hr and comparable capture of areas of change, containing 22% tetramer+ cells (Figure 7).
evidence: This is directly stated as a performance comparison and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: T-REX without dimensionality reduction (KNN on original features) was both slower (1.7 hr) and less accurate, identifying too many putative regions of change that were not tetramer+ hotspots.
source: Finally, we tested T-REX without dimensionality reduction, running KNN directly on the 14 original surface protein features previously utilized when performing either UMAP or t-SNE dimensionality reduction. This KNN on the original feature space was both slower (1.7 hr) and less accurate, in that it identified too many putative regions of change, most of which were not tetramer+ hotspots (Figure 7).
evidence: This is directly stated as a performance comparison and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: SPADE identified no regions of change ≥95% when tested on RV001 data.
source: When SPADE was tested using the 14 original features, no regions of change ≥95% were identified (Figure 7).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of algorithm comparison and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Phenograph using original features identified 13 clusters, none of which displayed significant change (average of 49% ± 6.4%) and none of which contained >5% tetramer+ cells.
source: Next, the KNN-based Phenograph algorithm was tested using the 14 original features and a k-value of 60 (as in T-REX, Figure 4). This test of Phenograph identified 13 clusters, none of which displayed significant change (average of 49% ± 6.4%) and none of which contained >5% tetramer+ cells.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of algorithm comparison.

claim: FlowSOM did not identify regions of change using either UMAP or original features (average of 50% ± 5%) and did not identify clusters with >5% tetramer+ cells.
source: FlowSOM did not identify regions of change using either UMAP or original features (average of 50% ± 5%) and did not identify clusters with >5% tetramer+ cells.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of algorithm comparison.

claim: Citrus required 3 hr and found 156 total clusters, with >30 being significantly associated with either day 0 or day 7 abundance, but only one cluster had >5% tetramer+ cells.
source: Finally, we used 10 subsamples of each day to test Citrus on RV001 as Citrus requires two groups and several samples per group. This test of Citrus required 3 hr and found 156 total clusters, with >30 being significantly associated with either day 0 or day 7 abundance. Of these significant clusters, only one had >5% tetramer+ cells.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of algorithm comparison.

claim: Phenotypes were comparable for all methods that identified at least one hotspot of >85% change, as quantified by RMSD analysis of MEM labels (ranged from 97.1 to 98.7).
source: Importantly, phenotypes were comparable for all methods that identified at least one hotspot of >85% change, as quantified by RMSD analysis of MEM labels (Greenplate et al., 2019) (ranged from 97.1 to 98.7, with 100 being the highest degree of similarity).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of quantitative phenotype comparison across methods.

claim: T-REX consistently identified tetramer+ hotspots across 10 subsamples, each containing 10% of the cells from RV001.
source: Finally, as an additional test of T-REX stability, sample RV001 was subsampled into 10 groups, each containing 10% of the cells. T-REX was then run using both the same original (common) UMAP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and subsample-specific (unique) UMAPs. In all cases of subsampling, T-REX consistently identified tetramer+ hotspots based on ≥90 % or ≥ 95 % change across the 10 subsamples.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of stability testing and supported by data in the referenced figure.

claim: Healthy adult volunteers were enrolled in an experimental rhinovirus infection study and judged to be seronegative to the challenge virus strain (RV-A16; serum neutralizing antibody titer ≤1:2).
source: Healthy adult volunteers (ages 18–40) were enrolled in an experimental rhinovirus infection study. All subjects were judged to be seronegative to the challenge virus strain (RV-A16; serum neutralizing antibody titer ≤1:2).
evidence: This is directly stated as a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Subjects were inoculated with 100 TCID50 of RV-A16 on study day 0.
source: Subjects were inoculated with 100 TCID50 of RV-A16 (FDA IND 15162) on study day 0 and were judged to be infected if they seroconverted to the challenge virus by study day 28 (≥4-fold increase in titer) and/or shed virus in nasal wash specimens during the first five days of infection, according to standard protocols (Muehling et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated as a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Two of the eight study subjects challenged with rhinovirus were not infected (RV002 and RV003).
source: Notably, two of the eight study subjects challenged with rhinovirus were not infected (RV002 and RV003); all other individuals were infected (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of the rhinovirus challenge study.

claim: Dataset 2 consisted of mass cytometry data from 12 COVID-19 patients with at least two blood samples over time.
source: Next, T-REX was applied to Dataset 2, a mass cytometry study of longitudinal collection of blood from patients with COVID-19 (Rodriguez et al., 2020). This study originally contained data for 39 total patients, of which 12 patients had accessible mass cytometry data with at least two blood samples over time.
evidence: This is directly stated as a description of Dataset 2.

claim: The rhinovirus challenge study was approved by the University of Virginia Human Investigations Committee and registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02796001).
source: Dataset 1 was a newly generated dataset of PBMCs obtained by longitudinal sampling of healthy volunteers who were challenged intranasally with RV-A16. The study was approved by the University of Virginia Human Investigations Committee, performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02796001).
evidence: This is directly stated as regulatory and ethical information about the study.

claim: After rhinovirus challenge, expanded regions displayed molecular signatures consistent with activated memory (CD45RO+ CD38+) and tissue trafficking (e.g., CCR5 enrichment).
source: Specifically, after rhinovirus challenge, expanded regions displayed molecular signatures consistent with activated memory (CD45RO + CD38+) and tissue trafficking (e.g., CCR5 enrichment in the MEM labels) that aligned with our previous findings for rhinovirus-specific CD4+ T cells using manual gating methods and a limited marker panel (Muehling et al., 2020; Wisniewski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of T-REX and MEM analysis and is consistent with prior cited studies.

claim: CD147 was highly expressed on many cells that changed during COVID-19 infection and was observed to change greatly on some populations over time.
source: Notably, CD147/Basigin was highly expressed on many cells that changed during infection and was observed to change greatly on some populations over time.
evidence: This is directly stated as an observation from T-REX analysis of COVID-19 data.

claim: CD147 has been proposed as both a binding partner for SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and a potential mechanism of cellular entry, although evidence is needed to support this controversial hypothesis.
source: CD147 has been proposed in pre-prints as both a binding partner for SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and a potential mechanism of cellular entry, although evidence is needed to support this controversial hypothesis (Shilts and Wright, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from the literature with a citation, noting it is controversial.

claim: In the study of Dataset 2, the authors noted that immune responses were dominated by cells expressing CD38 and CD147.
source: In the study of Dataset 2, the authors noted that immune responses were dominated by cells expressing CD38 and CD147 (Rodriguez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the original study of Dataset 2 with a citation.

claim: T-REX is designed for use on a pair of data files, such as pairs of timepoints.
source: T-REX was designed for use on a pair of data files, such as the pairs of timepoints tested here, but it can also be used for other paired comparisons.
evidence: This is directly stated as a description of T-REX design.

claim: T-REX is very sensitive to batch effects, and issues need to be addressed before analysis, or samples need to be analyzed in a batch-specific manner.
source: T-REX is also very sensitive to batch effects, and issues like these need to be addressed before analysis, or samples need to be analyzed in a batch-specific manner.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and consideration for using T-REX.

claim: MEM labels allow quantitative comparison across batches, instruments, and data types.
source: We expect that one advantage of using MEM labels to summarize the phenotype of T-REX populations is that MEM labels have been shown to allow quantitative comparison across batches, instruments, and data types (Diggins et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an expected advantage based on prior work cited.

claim: T-REX performance may depend on the number of cells and the algorithm was designed for studies with hundreds of thousands to millions of cells.
source: T-REX performance may depend on the number of cells and the algorithm was designed for studies with hundreds of thousands to millions of cells.
evidence: This is stated as a design consideration for T-REX.

claim: Analyses with fewer than 1000 cells are unlikely to be productive with T-REX.
source: Analyses with fewer than 1000 cells are unlikely to be productive, and analyses with fewer cells may require testing and adjusting k more than analyses with >100,000 cells.
evidence: This is stated as a practical limitation of T-REX.

claim: Tetramer+ hotspots were still detected with 100,000 cells per sample in subsampling tests.
source: In testing subsamples, tetramer+ hotspots were still detected with 100,000 cells per sample (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of subsampling analysis and supported by the referenced figure.

claim: The parameters chosen by the user in T-REX are the k-value, the markers used to create the UMAP, the markers used for MEM, and the DBSCAN settings.
source: The parameters that are chosen by the user are the k-value, the markers used to create the UMAP, the markers used for MEM, and the DBSCAN settings.
evidence: This is directly stated as a description of user-adjustable parameters in T-REX.

claim: T-REX combines UMAP, KNN, and Marker Enrichment Modeling (MEM) in a rapid, unsupervised analysis workflow for paired samples from one individual.
source: In addition to combining UMAP, KNN, and Marker Enrichment Modeling (MEM) in a rapid, unsupervised analysis workflow for paired samples from one individual, T-REX contrasts with prior approaches in its specific focus on the regions of great difference between samples.
evidence: This is directly stated as a description of the T-REX algorithm design.

claim: T-REX contrasts with prior approaches in its specific focus on the regions of great difference between samples.
source: In addition to combining UMAP, KNN, and Marker Enrichment Modeling (MEM) in a rapid, unsupervised analysis workflow for paired samples from one individual, T-REX contrasts with prior approaches in its specific focus on the regions of great difference between samples.
evidence: This is directly stated as a distinguishing feature of T-REX compared to other methods.

claim: The T-REX algorithm was blinded to tetramers during analysis so that they could subsequently be used to test algorithm performance.
source: The T-REX algorithm was blinded to tetramers during analysis so that they could subsequently be used to test algorithm performance.
evidence: This is directly stated as a methodological approach to validate T-REX.

claim: Degree of change was calculated as the sum of the percent of cells in the 5th and 95th hotspots of change.
source: Degree of change was calculated as the sum of the percent of cells in the 5th and 95th hotspots of change.
evidence: This is directly stated as a definition of the degree of change metric.

claim: Direction of change is the ratio of ≥95% expansion to contraction in the sample and was calculated as the difference between the number of cells in the 95th and 5th hotspots of change divided by the sum of the number of cells in the 95th and 5th hotspots of change.
source: Direction of change is the ratio of ≥95% expansion to contraction in the sample and was calculated as the difference between the number of cells in the 95th and 5th hotspots of change divided by the sum of the number of cells in the 95th and 5th hotspots of change.
evidence: This is directly stated as a definition of the direction of change metric.

claim: A negative direction of change value indicates that there was significant contraction that was more common than significant expansion.
source: A negative direction of change value indicates that there was significant contraction that was more common than significant expansion.
evidence: This is directly stated as an interpretation of the direction of change metric.

claim: The values for directionality range from 0.00 (evenly contracting and expanding) to ±1.00 (all contracting or expanding).
source: The values for directionality range from 0.00 (evenly contracting and expanding) to ±1.00 (all contracting or expanding).
evidence: This is directly stated as a description of the directionality metric range.

claim: Transparent analysis scripts for all four datasets and all presented results are publicly available on the CytoLab GitHub page for T-REX.
source: Transparent analysis scripts for all four datasets and all presented results are publicly available on the CytoLab GitHub page for T-REX (https://github.com/cytolab/T-REX) and include open-source code and commented Rmarkdown analysis walkthroughs.
evidence: This is directly stated as information about data and code availability.

claim: Rhinovirus Dataset 1 is available on FlowRepository (https://flowrepository.org/id/FR-FCM-Z2VX).
source: Rhinovirus Dataset 1 is a newly generated dataset created at the University of Virginia available on FlowRepository (https://flowrepository.org/id/FR-FCM-Z2VX).
evidence: This is directly stated as information about data availability.

claim: The optimal k-value for RV001 was determined to be 70 based on the inflection point of tetramer enrichment curves.
source: This approach identified the inflection point of the percent tetramer+ curve as k = 70 for RV001 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of k-value optimization analysis and supported by Figure 4.

claim: In further analysis of the remaining infected rhinovirus subjects, optimal k-values ranged from 30 to 80.
source: In further analysis of the remaining infected rhinovirus subjects, optimal k-values ranged from 30 to 80.
evidence: This is directly stated as a result of k-value optimization across subjects.

claim: A k-value of 60 was chosen and used in all other analyses of rhinovirus subjects as well as Datasets 2, 3, and 4.
source: A k-value of 60 was chosen and used in all other analyses of rhinovirus subjects (Figure 3), as well as Datasets 2, 3, and 4 described below.
evidence: This is directly stated as a methodological choice for consistency across analyses.

source: Furthermore, this strategy was able to enrich for tetramer+ cells in the one infected subject for which T-REX was unable to identify tetramer hotspots (RV007), and one in which the tetramer+ hotspot only met a ≥85% threshold of expansion (RV005), suggesting that T-REX-derived sorting strategies can be broadly applied across cohorts, including subjects whose response may not reach the threshold of identification by T-REX.

source: This observation was expected and is consistent with past tests of algorithms on detection of rare subsets, which found that over half the algorithms tested returned poor F1 accuracy scores for detecting known populations that were 0.8% or 0.03% of the cells in a sample (Weber and Robinson, 2016).

source: Notably, FlowSOM was a better performing algorithm in those examples.

claim: The 0.02% of virus-specific target cells in the rhinovirus study is connected to a larger population due to phenotypic similarity within the CD4+ T cell population.
source: An aspect of data structure in this study is the phenotypic similarity within the CD4+ T cell population, which means that the 0.02% of target cells is connected to a larger population and thus less apparent in the raw data.

claim: The threshold of change in T-REX removing the vast majority of cells that did not expand or contract ≥95% makes the virus-specific cells appear as separate clusters.
source: Thus, it is the threshold of change in T-REX removing the vast majority of cells (i.e., the cells that did not expand or contract ≥95%) that makes the virus-specific cells appear as separate clusters and greatly simplifies the task of distinguishing cluster groups.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why T-REX is effective at identifying rare cells.
